passage:
Paragraph A
Most people think of weather as something that happens within a few kilometres of the ground. Forecasters, however, also issue warnings for a second kind of weather, one that has no wind you can feel and no rain you can see. Space weather describes the variations in the environment between the Sun and the Earth, and it matters for an entirely practical reason: it disturbs the technologies that modern life is built on, both in orbit and on the surface.

Paragraph B
The background condition is the solar wind, which flows outward from the Sun continuously and consists mainly of protons and electrons in the state known as plasma. It is always blowing, and the Earth's magnetic field normally deflects it. What forecasters watch for are the departures from that steady state — the sudden events on the Sun that send radiation, particles or matter towards the Earth in quantities the magnetic field cannot simply turn aside.

Paragraph C
The first of these is the solar flare, a large eruption of electromagnetic radiation lasting from minutes to hours. Because the emission is light, it crosses to the Earth in the eight minutes that light itself takes, which means the flare arrives at the same moment as the first evidence of it. The X-rays and extreme ultraviolet ionise the lower layers of the ionosphere on the sunlit side of the planet, and high-frequency radio signals that would normally reflect from that region are absorbed instead. The result is a radio blackout. Even a minor one degrades communication on the daylit hemisphere and causes occasional loss of contact, while low-frequency navigation signals deteriorate for short intervals.

Paragraph D
A second class of event follows within minutes to hours. When a large magnetic eruption accelerates charged particles in the solar atmosphere to very high velocities, the protons among them can reach the Earth in minutes. Such a solar radiation storm is a hazard chiefly to anything outside the shelter of the lower atmosphere: satellites, astronauts, and aircraft flying polar routes where the magnetic field offers least protection.

Paragraph E
The slowest and most consequential events are coronal mass ejections — large expulsions of plasma and magnetic field from the Sun's corona, carrying billions of tonnes of material. Their speeds vary enormously, from under 250 kilometres per second to nearly three thousand, so that the fastest arrive in fifteen to eighteen hours while the slowest take several days. When one strikes and the energy of the solar wind is transferred efficiently into the space surrounding the Earth, the result is a geomagnetic storm: a major disturbance of the magnetosphere.

Paragraph F
Geomagnetic storms are felt on the ground because a changing magnetic field induces currents in long conductors, and few conductors are longer than a national electricity grid. These induced currents can saturate transformers, which were designed for alternating current and behave badly when a slow direct current is added. The consequences are not hypothetical. In March 1989 a storm collapsed the Hydro-Québec network in about ninety seconds and left several million people without power for around nine hours. The largest storm on record, in 1859, disrupted telegraph lines at a time when there was almost nothing else electrical to disrupt.

Paragraph G
In orbit the effects are different and more varied. Energetic particles degrade solar panels and can flip bits in onboard electronics; the ionosphere's disturbance introduces errors into satellite navigation signals; and a storm heats and expands the upper atmosphere, so that satellites in low orbits encounter more gas than expected. That last effect, satellite drag, shortens orbital lifetimes and forces operators to recalculate the positions of everything they are tracking.

Paragraph H
Forecasting is complicated by an awkward asymmetry. The events that arrive first are the ones there is no time to warn about, since a flare travels at the speed of light; the events that can be warned about are the ones that take a day or more to cross the gap. Spacecraft stationed far upstream of the Earth sample the solar wind directly, but only about an hour before it reaches us, which is enough to alert a grid operator and not much more. Space weather forecasting therefore remains a matter of watching the Sun for the eruption, estimating a speed and a direction, and accepting a wide margin of error until the storm is almost overhead.

(Glossary: plasma: a gas so hot that its atoms have separated into charged particles; ionosphere: the electrically charged upper region of the atmosphere; magnetosphere: the region around the Earth controlled by its magnetic field; corona: the outermost layer of the Sun's atmosphere.)
